title: Who Put Bella In the Wych Elm?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the 1943 discovery of a woman's skeleton in a witch elm in Hagley Wood near Birmingham, England, known as the "Bella in the Witch Elm" case. Topics include the teenage boys who found the skull, pathologist James Webster's findings, the chalk graffiti asking "who put Bella in the witch elm," the Una Mosspup (Una Hainsworth) account blaming Jack Mosspup's Dutch friend Van Raalt, the witchcraft theory promoted by Margaret Murray, the hand of glory myth, Donald McCormick's fabricated claims, and the 2013 Independent theory linking Clara Bowerley and Joseph Jakobs. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about John Williams borrowing from classical works.
topics: graffiti who put Bella in the witch elm

entities.name: The Witch Cult in Western Europe

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the show with a tribute to Jonathan Strickland and some chatter about a colleague's visit to the office.

segments.title: Introduction to the Bella case
segments.summary: Josh introduces the famous true crime case and notes the witchcraft myths surrounding it. Chuck summarizes how four teenage boys found a skull in a tree in Hagley Wood in April 1943 while foraging during wartime rationing.

segments.title: Police investigation and pathologist's findings
segments.summary: Tommy Willetts told his parents and police were called. Pathologist James Webster examined the remains, estimating a woman around 35 and about five feet tall, and concluded it was likely murder based on fabric in the jaw and the tight opening. The case went cold after missing persons searches found no match.

segments.title: Chalk graffiti and reopened investigation
segments.summary: In March 1944 anonymous chalk graffiti appeared around Birmingham asking who put Bella in the witch elm. Police reopened the case, traced a shoe to a Lancashire company, and checked pear sales. A variant name Lubella also appeared and led nowhere.
topics: who put Bella in the witch elm graffiti

segments.title: Credit cards tangent
segments.summary: A brief tangent on the origins of credit cards, with the hosts guessing Diners Club and mentioning Telly Savalas.

segments.title: Witch elm name and Margaret Murray's witchcraft theory
segments.summary: The name witch elm derives from an old English word meaning smooth or supple, not witches. Folklorist Margaret Murray linked the murder to witchcraft and tree worship while investigating another case in 1945, which had been the killing of Charles Walton.

segments.title: Hand of glory myth
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the hand of glory was a burglar's superstition involving a candle-holding severed hand, and that no severed hand was found in the original police reports, a detail added later by some writers.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the story resumes.

segments.title: Wilfrid Jones and the anonymous letter
segments.summary: Journalist Wilfrid Byford Jones, writing as Quaestor, published speculative articles. A reader signing as Una of Claverley wrote in, claiming the killer died insane in 1942 and the victim was a Dutch woman who arrived illegally in England around 1941. Police tracked her down.

segments.title: Una Hainsworth's account
segments.summary: Una Mosspup, later Una Hainsworth, told police her husband Jack brought home Van Raalt, a Dutch friend and alleged Nazi spy. Jack was drunk after an evening with Van Raalt and a Dutch woman who passed out in the car, and Van Raalt suggested placing her in the tree. Jack later declined mentally and died in a mental hospital in 1942. The hosts find her account credible.

segments.title: Donald McCormick's fabricated book
segments.summary: Writer Donald McCormick's 1968 book Murder by Witchcraft claimed an anonymous interview and Nazi files identifying the victim as a Dutch-born German spy named Clara Bella. The book popularized photos of a tree that was later cut down and may not have been a witch elm.

segments.title: Josh's childhood memory of the book
segments.summary: Josh recalls seeing the photos in a book as a child, and the hosts joke about nostalgia.

segments.title: Joseph Jakobs and the 2013 Independent theory
segments.summary: A 2013 Independent article linked the case to German spy Joseph Jakobs, captured in 1941 near Cambridge with a photo of Clara Landau, actually Clara Bowerley, a cabaret singer. The Independent proposed Clara Bella as the victim. Bowerley was about six feet tall and died in a German hospital a year after the murder, undermining the theory.

segments.title: Giselle Jakobs research and lost DNA evidence
segments.summary: Giselle Jakobs, a PhD in ancient history, researched the case on a website. Any DNA evidence from the 1940s and 1950s is believed lost after moving through different boxes and labs.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Josh recommends caution with sources on the case and transitions to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail on John Williams
segments.summary: A listener named Lad writes that John Williams borrows heavily from classical works, citing Stravinsky's Rite of Spring and Jaws. The hosts discuss The Lost Boys and thank the listener.
